episodes.episode_title: Mazumdar-Shaw's bold biotech mission: Affordable, accessible healthcare
episodes.listening_range: Approximately the first 26 minutes of a 34 minute episode, from her opening account of the journey to her answer on resilience. The transcript carries no timecodes, so this is estimated from speech rate. The transcript file holds only this section and the spoken start and end lines are noted at the top of it.
episodes.the_idea: Mazumdar-Shaw started Biocon in the 1970s, when India had no biotech industry, no funding for it, and few people who would back a young woman running a science company. She had no positional power to draw on. She built it by pulling in young scientists fresh out of the IITs and by getting the government to create a start-up fund that did not exist. Her people rule is blunt: hire minds that have not already been told how it is done, give an ordinary person a problem they can crack, and they turn into an extraordinary one. Her line on resilience is that it is not about her holding on. It is about whether the team holds on, which she says is her job to make happen.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The three questions draw from the section saved in this file, roughly the first 26 minutes of the episode. Focus on three things. First, how she built Biocon from nothing, with no industry and little capital: the young IIT scientists she pulled in and the government fund she pushed for, which became BIRAC. Second, her way of building and developing people: the problem-solver culture, why she favors fresh graduates over experienced hires, and what she means by ordinary people becoming extraordinary. Third, what she says resilience really is and whose job it is. You can skip the enzyme-to-drug, biosimilars, and Mylan acquisition details, which are about strategy, not people.

questions.question: Biocon started when India had no biotech industry and little money for one. Name two specific things Mazumdar-Shaw did to get it off the ground, including what she pushed the government to set up.

She says she would rather develop someone fresh from university than hire experienced people who arrive with the mindset of this is how we did it there. Name one role on your team where you made the opposite choice, and what it cost you.
Mazumdar-Shaw says resilience is not about her enduring but about making her team endure. Where does putting the weight on the team break down, and who carries it when the team cannot?

episodes.episode_title: THE LEADERSHIP LIST - L. David Marquet - Turn The Ship Around! (Episode Two)
episodes.listening_range: A marked section of about 15 minutes from a roughly 35 minute episode. The transcript carries no timecodes, so both figures are estimated from speech rate. The transcript file holds only this section and the spoken start and end lines are noted at the top of it.
episodes.the_idea: Marquet took the USS Santa Fe, a nuclear submarine rated worst in the fleet, to first. He did it by refusing to give orders. He calls the old way leader-follower and his way leader-leader. Instead of asking permission, his crew stated intent: I intend to submerge the ship. Ownership moved to the person doing the work. The outside-domain value here is a crew that has to hold together under real stress, where a missed step is not a bad quarter but a sunk boat. His claim that the change starts with the boss biting his own tongue, not with a speech about initiative, is the part that travels.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: The three questions draw from the marked stretch saved in this file, the core of the leadership section. Focus on three things. First, the four things Marquet says the military already had that let him hand decisions to the crew, and why they mattered. Second, the I intend to move: what the crew said instead of asking permission, and what it changed. Third, his account of why intent-based teams move faster and miss fewer steps under combat stress, including the example he uses. You can skip the opening about submarine classes and anything after the many minds exchange.

questions.question: Marquet names the things the military already had that let him hand decisions to the crew. Name at least two, and say what the crew started saying instead of asking permission.

Marquet says the change starts with the leader biting his own tongue, not with a speech. Name one decision you now make that a team member could state as intent instead, and what you would have to stop doing.
On a submarine the task is well defined and the stakes are physical. Where on your team would pushing decisions down like this backfire, and what would have to be true first?

episodes.episode_title: Unlocking the Secret Power of Groups with Colin Fisher
episodes.listening_range: Approximately 00:06:06 to 00:30:41 of a 42 minute episode, about 25 minutes of listening. The transcript file holds only this section and the publisher timecodes are noted at the top of it.
episodes.the_idea: This course is built on getting teams to cohere. Fisher, a group-dynamics researcher at University College London and a former jazz trumpeter, spends his time on the opposite finding: for decades the research kept showing that groups came in under the sum of their parts. He calls these process losses, and they show up in rope-pulling, cheering, stuffing envelopes, and brainstorming. Groups only beat individuals under specific conditions, mostly when the task is complex and needs varied expertise. For well-worn tasks you are better off alone. He also says a working meeting should not pass about seven people, and that inviting people so they feel included is how you get rooms where no one is really heard. It is a useful check on the reflex to put every problem in a group.
episodes.what_will_be_assessed: This transcript has timestamps, so you can go straight to what is assessed. The marked stretch runs from about 06:06 to about 30:41. Focus on three things. First, what Fisher means by process losses, with the examples he gives of groups coming in under the sum of their parts, and the conditions under which groups do beat individuals. Second, his rule about meeting size and why he says inviting people to be included backfires. Third, why he says competition inside a team is hard to make healthy. You do not need the intro, the remote and hybrid section after 30:41, or the closing about his hobbies.

questions.question: Fisher says that for years research found groups were less than the sum of their parts. Name two of the examples he gives, and name the main condition under which a group does beat individuals.

Fisher says a working meeting should not have more than about seven people, and that inviting people to be nice produces rooms where no one is heard. Name one recurring meeting of yours that fails this test, and who you would take off the list.

Fisher says that for well-defined, familiar tasks an individual usually beats a group. Where has this course's push for teamwork led you to convene a group you did not need, and how would you tell the difference next time?
